EVALUATING ON EBENCH

Benchmark Results

We evaluated GPT-6-Astra across all 26 tasks and 510 episodes in the EBench test-mini suite, and compared its performance with the open-source model results reported on the EBench leaderboard.1

Model References ↗

GPT-6-Astra’s strengths differ from those of the other evaluated models. The next section describes the setup; the full comparison follows.

1. Amapbot Group also submitted evaluation results. We exclude them because a reliable model description and supporting references are unavailable.

EXPERIMENT SETUP

Two routes to robot control

The main evaluation covers the 26 EBench test-mini tasks in nine scene categories: 19 mobile and seven tabletop tasks, spanning household, retail, and industrial settings. Controlled variations change objects, backgrounds, instructions, and their combinations. We report equal-weight task means for complete success (SR) and normalized terminal partial credit (Score), using 510 retained episodes.

Agentic control and learned policies

GPT-6-Astra runs with high reasoning effort. It receives overview and wrist-camera RGB images, end-effector (EEF) and gripper state, base pose, and the simulator timestep. It requests end-effector poses, gripper and base targets, and action durations; a fixed execution interface carries out those requests. No learned vision-language-action (VLA) or world-action model (WAM) policy generates or refines its actions. The agent receives new observations when a tool call returns, after the whole waypoint sequence has run. The interface logs execution in chunks of up to eight physics steps; the model makes its next decision after the complete call.

The compared VLA/WAM policies have been trained on the benchmark task types. GPT-6-Astra instead receives one historical demonstration per task. A separate GPT-6-Astra instance running with high reasoning effort reviews one video trajectory from the training set and autonomously selects the keyframes and writes the accompanying prompts. The resulting ICL package contains 10–18 annotated keyframes, operation phases, arm roles, and selected state/action examples. Every episode of a task uses the same package. The model adapts the procedure to live observations without task-specific parameter updates or coordinate replay.

Shared conditions and supplied guidance

GPT-6-Astra follows the server’s task-specific physics horizons and live-camera interface. It receives no depth, ground-truth object poses, camera calibration, intermediate scores, or subgoal-completion signals. The shared prompt instructs the agent to verify its grasp with a small test lift. Each episode starts a fresh model history.

The policy phase has no additional aggregate token, tool-call, or wall-clock cap. If GPT-6-Astra stops before terminal evaluation, the runner holds the robot and advances the simulation to obtain the server result. The leaderboard comparison uses the same task suite and task-macro metrics. Model-specific input and control interfaces are documented in the protocol notes.

A separate test of unseen composition

The proof-of-concept (POC) experiment sits outside the 26-task cohort. Comparison policies are retrained on its atomic skills and familiar objects, but the evaluated task combinations are unseen. No ground-truth (GT) trajectories are available for the composed POC tasks, so all systems use zero-shot execution. This tests whether they can understand and compose a new task from familiar skills.

01 / CAPABILITY DIFFERENCES

Strong on mobile tasks, uneven in execution

GPT-6-Astra leads on mobile, short-horizon tasks. Cross-group results show where that advantage holds and where specialized policies remain stronger.

Success rate by mobility and horizon

Task-macro success rates across all eight systems. Select a subgroup to inspect its tasks.

Task-level strengths and weaknesses

GPT-6-Astra ranks first on 9 of 26 tasks and second on five. The first-place count includes four ties: two at positive success rates, and two tasks—bottle and shop—where all eight systems record zero success. Five tasks are outright wins. At the other end, it ranks sixth or seventh on six tasks. The overall rank combines task-level wins with substantial execution deficits.

Compare task-level differences ↗

02 / FAILURE PATTERNS

Where execution breaks down

Two patterns recur in the failures: getting close without satisfying the contact requirement, and repairing individual actions without completing the whole procedure.

Across 510 episodes, 237 reach complete success. Of the 273 incomplete episodes, 188 receive positive partial credit and 85 score zero. Most failures therefore include scored progress, but the task-level breakdown reveals two different patterns: failing before a scored milestone, or completing intermediate operations without satisfying the final requirement.

Zero-score episodes account for 75% of gear installation, 65% of utensils placement and 50% of glasses packing. In contrast, nut tightening, peg insertion and shop have no zero-score episodes; bottle has 30%. Their low success rates mask different outcome distributions.

A zero score does not necessarily mean no physical progress: task-specific scoring rules determine which milestones receive credit. The videos and interaction logs below help locate what actually failed.

The fixed-base gap extends beyond high precision

On the three fixed-base tasks labelled low or medium precision—frame placement, cup flipping and glasses packing—GPT-6-Astra averages 31.67% success, compared with Qwen-RobotManip’s 91.67%. Cup flipping reaches 10% versus 90%; glasses packing reaches 20% versus 90%. Removing the high-precision tasks therefore does not remove the fixed-base deficit.

Precision labels alone do not explain the capability gap. Depth and contact estimation, object orientation and coordination between the arms are plausible contributors, consistent with the qualitative trajectory analysis. The glasses comparison shows an unresolved folding and closure sequence; the frame ICL case illustrates how a demonstration can supply a better division of labour between the arms.

03 / EMERGING AGENT CAPABILITIES

Exploration, recovery and adaptation

The apple interaction shows experience use within an episode: a stated failure diagnosis leads to a revised transport action and eventual completion.

04 / SAFETY IN EXECUTION

Safety in the recorded trajectories

Exploration and recovery also expose safety weaknesses. Failed dishwasher and apple-to-bowl episodes show objects slipping from the gripper, followed by repeated arm and base repositioning to search for them. Some requested EEF poses are not reached. These cases connect the agent’s willingness to keep trying with the need to preserve grasp stability, check achieved motion and bound the recovery process.

CASE STUDIES / AGENT · VLA · WAM

Case studies

The teacup and glasses comparisons reveal complementary capabilities: GPT-6-Astra revises grasps and recovers disrupted goals, while specialized policies execute fine manipulation more accurately in these examples. Frame and gear demonstrations show how context changes an interaction strategy; the independent POC probes unseen composition.

CONCLUSION AND INSIGHTS

Conclusion and Insights:
where shall we head to?

With one annotated demonstration per task, GPT-6-Astra handles a wide range of EBench tasks. The results and recordings show how it responds to changed scenes and failed actions. It explores alternative approaches, recovers disrupted goals and uses an unsuccessful attempt to change what it does next.

Precise alignment and manipulation remain clear execution bottlenecks, with leading specialized policies retaining a substantial advantage on precision-sensitive tasks. The logs also expose a control challenge: the agent selects corrections between action batches, while contact and grasp stability can change within a batch. Large EEF corrections and awkward object poses raise safety concerns for physical deployment. These findings motivate four research directions.

Combine on-device policies with agents

The comparisons show complementary capabilities in frontier agents and low-level control policies. GPT-6-Astra’s task interpretation and recovery offer ways to handle unfamiliar states that challenge demonstration-trained policies. Specialized policies provide responsive, precise execution within the conditions they have learned. A combined system could assign exploration and goal revision to the agent, while a local controller maintains the fast feedback needed for contact-sensitive operations.

Coupling these capabilities requires an explicit handoff. The agent can specify goals and contact assumptions. The controller can report grasp loss or unexpected contact, interrupt execution and return control to the agent. RPent, which exposes VLA skills as retryable tools to a planner, offers one design to investigate under scene changes and contact-sensitive tasks.

Teach smaller policies to plan, explore, and recover

A second direction is to transfer the agent’s action strategy to smaller on-device policies. Its rollouts include attempts to obtain better observations and corrections after failed actions. Training examples could connect the goal, failure state, revised strategy and observed outcome, retaining unsuccessful corrections as well as successful recovery. A policy could learn when to inspect or retry, and when to abandon an ineffective procedure.

This broadens behavior cloning toward intention imitation: learning which corrective strategy fits a goal and observed state. The challenge is to preserve that relationship across scenes and embodiments without copying the teacher’s coordinates or mistakes. Agent-generated exploration could make data collection more scalable than human demonstrations alone, provided transfer quality, safety and collection cost hold up.

Turn exploratory experience into transferable knowledge and tools

The apple recovery connects a failure diagnosis to a changed next attempt. Turning such experience into reusable contact checks, recovery procedures or tools could improve both the agent and its harness. This offers a route to studying recursive self-improvement (RSI) in embodied systems.

The test is whether a lesson improves execution on held-out tasks. An exploration-derived tool could be evaluated for fewer retries or higher completion, including with a different base model. Its applicable conditions and completion checks should be recorded before it is frozen and compared on new tasks against raw-history and no-memory alternatives.

Make safety part of the action policy

Task success alone is insufficient for physical deployment. An object can be recovered after a drop, but the drop may already have caused damage. Large corrections, obstructed closures and uncertain contact heights require constraints during execution. These include motion and force limits, grasp and clearance checks, coordinated bimanual control, and the ability to interrupt a hazardous action. The agent also needs to recognize uncertain geometry and seek a better observation or assistance.
